summary: Describes how to use the Boneh-Franklin and Boneh-Boyen identity-based encryption algorithms in the Cryptographic Message Syntax to protect content-encryption keys. It defines object identifiers and how to encode a recipient's identity. This is an informational document.

eli5.summary: This shows how to use two particular secret-sending recipes, where an email address is the key, inside the standard format for secure messages.

subtitle: Identity-based encryption for encrypted email messages

tldr.problem: Email applications need a standard way to apply identity-based encryption to protect messages. Different implementations need to agree on data formats and structures.
tldr.mechanism: This document specifies how to use the Boneh-Franklin and Boneh-Boyen IBE algorithms within CMS (Cryptographic Message Syntax), the standard format for secure messages. It defines the object identifiers for each algorithm, how to encode a recipient's email identity, and the exact processing steps for senders and receivers.
tldr.outcome: Email applications can now interoperably encrypt messages to a recipient's email address and include time-based key lifetimes that require periodic re-authentication. Senders no longer need to obtain keys beforehand.

today: RFC 5409 is an Informational document. It works with RFC 5408, which defines the IBE architecture, and RFC 5091, which defines the cryptographic algorithms. This RFC enables interoperable IBE-encrypted email by specifying how to combine IBE with the standard CMS message format.

sections.title: IBE Algorithms for Email
sections.content:
This document specifies how to use two identity-based encryption algorithms, Boneh-Franklin (BF) and Boneh-Boyen (BB1), within CMS, the standard message format for secure email and other encrypted content. Instead of encrypting the full message directly, IBE encrypts the content-encryption key (CEK), the random key that actually protects the message data.

Because IBE allows the sender to derive the recipient's public key from their email address alone, senders no longer need to obtain or look up keys beforehand. The recipient obtains their private key from a Private Key Generator (PKG) only when needed, after authenticating.
sections.eli5: This document shows how to use two specific IBE recipes inside the standard way of sending encrypted email, so the sender can use just the recipient's email address as the encryption key.

sections.title: Data Structures for IBE in CMS
sections.content:
An IBE-encrypted message in CMS uses the OtherRecipientInfo field to hold IBE-specific information. The sender fills in an IBERecipientInfo structure with several required fields. The cmsVersion is always 3. The keyFetchMethod is an object identifier that tells the receiver which key-fetching protocol to use; it SHOULD be set to uriPPSOID, which directs the receiver to the Public Parameter Server's URI.

The recipientIdentity is a DER-encoded IBEIdentityInfo that contains the district (the URI where public parameters are published), a serial number identifying this particular set of parameters, an identity type, and identity data. For email, the identityType MUST be cmsIdentityOID, and the identityData MUST be an EmailIdentityData structure containing the recipient's email address in rfc822 format and a time value.

The time field deserves special attention. This is the 'not-before' time, usually set to when the message is encrypted, but it can be set to a future time. It enables a key-lifetime mechanism: when rounded to a time interval (such as one week), the recipient only needs to request one IBE private key per interval rather than one per message, while still requiring periodic re-authentication. The PKG SHOULD NOT issue keys too far into the future, to prevent stolen credentials from being used to request all future keys at once.
sections.eli5: The message says 'this email address can open me, and use the key that was created around this time.' The time lets you use the same key for a whole day or week instead of getting a new key for every message.

sections.title: Encrypting and Decrypting Messages
sections.content:
A sender encrypts an IBE message by first choosing which IBE public parameters to use according to their local security policy. The sender looks up the URI where those parameters live. The sender then sets all the fields of IBERecipientInfo: the district URI, a serial number, the recipient's email address and time, and the keyFetchMethod OID. The sender computes the recipient's IBE public key from these values and the public parameters, encrypts the CEK with that key using either the Boneh-Franklin or Boneh-Boyen algorithm, and sets the encryptedKey field to the result. Finally, the sender sets the CMS keyEncryptionAlgorithm field to the OID for the algorithm used (bf or bb1).

A receiver processes the message by first recognizing from the oriType field that it is IBE-encrypted. The receiver extracts the recipientIdentity to find which district and time to use. The receiver fetches the IBE public parameters from the district URI using the process defined in RFC 5408. The receiver then authenticates to the Private Key Generator and requests the private key for the extracted identity and time. Once the receiver has the private key and the public parameters, they decrypt the CEK using the Boneh-Franklin or Boneh-Boyen algorithm, then decrypt the message content with the CEK.
sections.eli5: The sender builds a label with the email address and time, uses it to make an encryption key, and sends the encrypted message with that label. The receiver reads the label, asks the trusted server for their private key for that label and time, then unlocks the message.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security of IBE in CMS depends on the same assumptions as the IBE architecture itself and the underlying cryptographic algorithms. All communication with the PPS and PKG MUST use TLS to protect authentication credentials and private keys in transit. If the PKG's master secret is compromised, all past and future messages are at risk of decryption. Administrators of a PKG should implement strong controls, such as requiring multiple administrators to approve key generation, and should maintain audit logs of all security-critical events.

The PKG inherently has the ability to decrypt any message by generating private keys, so PKG administrators must be trustworthy. An IBE system SHOULD implement multi-administrator controls and auditing to minimize the risk of insider abuse. The strength of user authentication to the PKG is also critical; if an attacker guesses an IBE user's credentials, they can request private keys and decrypt that user's messages.
sections.eli5: The trusted server that gives out keys has a lot of power, so you must protect it and trust its administrators. If someone steals your password to the key server, they can get your keys and read your old messages.
